description:
Welcome to Kuka's Crew! 

We are university students participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our goal is to develop software that helps astronauts monitor their health during long-duration space missions. 

We are passionate about technology, programming, and space exploration. Through teamwork and creativity, we aim to build a practical solution that collects, analyzes, and visualizes health data. 

Our mission is to bring innovation closer to space!
summary:
AVEGA is a software layer that works on top of existing astronaut sensors and NASA health measures and looks at mind and body together. It brings physiological data (heart rate, sleep, symptoms, cabin CO2, radiation dose) and psychological data (daily check-ins, VAS self-ratings, cognitive scores and our own creative and interactive tasks) into one place and compares each astronaut with their own baseline.

Its core is the link between psychological state and physical health in each person: AVEGA shows in plain words how strongly they move together (for example, “on high-stress days your heart rate is 1.1 bpm higher”), tracks 7-day trends and flags early risks. Because a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way on a Mars mission, an on-board assistant works offline: it interviews the astronaut, checks the answers against their data, gives first-step recommendations with a source for each, sets an urgency level and prepares a summary for the flight surgeon.

AVEGA does not replace NASA’s medical and psychological support; it complements it with a more personal analysis. All data in the prototype are synthetic; it gives no diagnosis and no medication advice.
details:
The idea
AVEGA - Integrated Astronaut Health & Crew Well-being Monitoring System

AVEGA is a health-monitoring system designed to help astronauts monitor their physical and psychological well-being during long space missions.

The idea behind AVEGA is that physical and psychological health are closely connected. Changes in one can affect the other, so looking at them separately may not provide a complete understanding of an astronaut's condition.

To address this, AVEGA brings together physiological and psychological data. It uses existing research, NASA-related health monitoring approaches, and established assessment methods to examine individual patterns, identify possible risks, and provide recommendations based on each astronaut's usual condition.

What AVEGA does

Personal health monitoring. AVEGA tracks indicators such as heart rate, sleep, mood, stress, energy, and cognitive performance. Rather than comparing astronauts with general population averages, the system uses each person's baseline measurements to identify changes that may be meaningful for them.

Mind and body connection. AVEGA looks at how physical and psychological indicators may be related. For example, it can show whether periods of increased stress occur alongside changes in heart rate or sleep quality. This helps users see patterns that might be harder to notice when looking at each indicator separately.

Early risk detection. The system compares recent measurements with an astronaut's usual condition. It highlights negative trends and changes that may need further attention. These results are intended to support monitoring, not to provide a medical diagnosis.

Offline assistant. Communication with Earth may be delayed during deep-space missions, so AVEGA includes an assistant that can operate without a constant connection. It asks astronauts about their condition, considers their answers alongside available health data, and provides basic recommendations. If something appears to require attention, it can help prepare a summary for the flight surgeon.

Psychological assessment. In addition to NASA-based assessment approaches, we developed two interactive activities of our own: Creative Task and Crew Connection. Creative Task explores aspects of emotional and cognitive well-being, while Crew Connection focuses on relationships and communication within the crew. These are experimental methods developed for our project, not validated NASA assessment instruments.

Radiation monitoring. AVEGA also includes a radiation exposure model based on NASA-related reference data. It allows users to view dose rates and cumulative exposure over time.

What makes AVEGA different

AVEGA does more than collect individual health measurements. It brings different indicators together and looks for patterns specific to each astronaut.

For example, an astronaut may experience changes in sleep quality at the same time as increased stress or changes in physical measurements. Looking at these indicators together can help identify possible connections and give the astronaut and medical specialists more context when reviewing their condition.

We are particularly interested in psychosomatic and somatopsychic relationships: how psychological conditions may affect physical health, and how physical changes may influence psychological well-being. AVEGA is designed to explore these relationships through individual monitoring over time.

Why this matters for NASA

We recognize that NASA already has established medical and psychological support systems for astronauts. AVEGA is not intended to replace them. Our goal is to complement existing approaches by connecting different types of health data and showing how they may change together.

Long space missions bring challenges that go beyond physical demands. Isolation, limited personal space, communication delays, and prolonged time away from Earth can all affect an astronaut's well-being and performance. These factors influenced our approach to AVEGA.

By tracking individual changes over time, the system may help astronauts notice patterns earlier and give medical specialists additional information when assessing a crew member's condition.

How we built it

AVEGA was developed as an offline single-page application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used Python for synthetic data generation and build scripts, while Playwright was used for automated testing.

The system applies basic statistical methods, including personal averages, standard deviations, correlations, and short-term trend analysis. Its development draws on NASA Human Research Program materials, Spaceflight Standard Measures, and scientific publications.

All data used in the prototype are synthetic and clearly labelled. We also distinguish between established assessment methods and the experimental activities developed by our team. AVEGA does not provide medical diagnoses or medication recommendations.

Our vision

We believe that monitoring astronaut health requires looking at more than separate physical measurements. Emotional well-being, cognitive performance, physical condition, and relationships within the crew can all influence one another.

AVEGA brings these areas together in one system. Our goal is to give astronauts a clearer view of their own condition and provide medical specialists with additional context when supporting crews during long-duration space missions.
